blocks.h: FIFTY-ONE MINUTES IN FULL SUN
Roya Publication No. 121
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

Fifty-one minutes is the length of a telephone call. A man took it on a summer morning twenty-six years ago, standing beside a road in full sun, and he has kept the record of it ever since. He can tell you the number. He cannot tell you why he kept it.

Rostam Bina makes one medicine. Forty million Americans take it every Thursday with a glass of water, and so does he. His company is worth more than every airline in the country, and most of that worth sits in the retirement funds of teachers and nurses. For twenty years the magazines have called him the calm man. People did not put their savings in a tablet. They put them in him.

Then a newspaper prints a photograph of Rostam at the door of a house on the coast, with a woman who is not his wife. Ninety billion dollars are gone in a morning. The board wants an apology on film. Thirty-five takes in a studio have all come out the same: smooth, correct, and sorry about nothing.

So the crew is sent home. One camera operator comes to his house instead, and she has one condition. There will be no script. Every Thursday he will sit down and say what he did, from the beginning, in his own words.
He agrees. It seems efficient.
He has a great deal to say. She has not told him why she asked for the job.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR
This book began with one question. What if we did not feel remorse for our past mistakes?

I do not mean forgetting them. I mean remembering every one of them clearly and feeling nothing when we do. I wondered what kind of person that would make. Part of me thought it might make a stronger one. A person like that could take risks without flinching. He could fail in public on Monday and begin again on Tuesday. He could chase one goal for thirty years and never lose a night’s sleep over something he did on the way. Much of what we call drive, and some of what we call creativity, may be only this: a lighter load.

Then I asked the second question. Would that person ever learn anything? We like to think we avoid a wrong act because we know it is wrong. I am no longer sure of that. We may avoid it because we remember how the last one felt.

The story came to me in a single week. Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, said publicly that he had been unfaithful to his wife. His board opened an investigation into reports that he had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Within days he had resigned from the company he built. As I write, that investigation has not reported, and I know no more than anyone else does.

What stayed with me was not the man. It was the speed. For years he had been one of the most admired builders alive, and people had put more than their money in him. It took less than a week. I watched it and thought that we should stop putting human beings on podiums. We never see their ordinary days. We do not know what they want when nobody is looking, or what they carry.

Nothing in this book is about him. Rostam Bina is invented. So are his company, his family, the town of Tres Olmos and every person in it. No medicine like his exists. Researchers have studied whether the pain of a memory can be dulled while the memory itself is kept. That work is real and it is careful. The tablet in this book is neither.
This is a dark book. It tells of harm to children, a suicide, and violence against a woman, and it tells them plainly.
I do not know the answer to my question. I only know which answer I am hoping for.
Chew Z
TAKE 36

It is Thursday. I take one tablet on Thursdays, with water. Forty million Americans do the same. I have done it for twenty-six years. She waits until the glass is empty. She takes the glass. She goes behind the camera.

The room is the long room at the back of my house. One chair. One table. One light. The window behind me is covered with a grey cloth. The camera stands on three legs. A red lamp on its front shows when it is recording. It is recording.
My name is Rostam Bina [ROS-tam bee-NAA]. In America I am called Ross. I am sixty-three. This is the thirty-sixth time I have made this statement.

The first thirty-five were made in the company’s studio. There was a crew of nine. A woman from the communications office held up cards. The board watched all thirty-five. The board said they were smooth. It said the public needed a man who was sorry and was getting a man reading the weather. I did not see the difference. I read the cards as written.

The crew was dismissed. The operator asked for the job and I gave it to her. Her condition was no script. Each Thursday I sit down and say what I did, from the beginning, in my own words. She films it. When there is one the board can use, we stop.
I agreed. It is efficient.
Item one.

For fourteen months I had sexual relations with a woman who is not my wife. The woman’s name is Helen. I have been married for thirty-four years. My wife lives in Oregon. We speak on the first Sunday of each month. We have never divorced. The public found that reassuring, so neither of us corrected it.
The size of this depends on what I am. I will state it.

I make one medicine. The company makes it. I started the company. Forty million people in this country take the medicine once a week. That is one adult in six. There are more abroad. The company is worth more than every airline in America put together. Most of that worth is held in retirement funds, by teachers and bus drivers and nurses. When the story about Helen appeared, the share price fell eleven per cent in one morning. That is ninety billion dollars. A teacher in Fresno lost four thousand of them before she got out of bed.

That is why there is a camera. Men do what I did every day and nobody films them. For twenty years the magazines have called me the calm man. The calm man eats the same lunch every day. He has had the same wife for thirty-four years. He has never raised his voice in a meeting. People do not put their retirement in a medicine. They put it in a man.
There is an earring in my car. I will come to it.

Helen was the first person the company ever paid. The company was then a rented unit behind a tyre shop in South San Francisco. It was my brother, a refrigerator, and me. She was twenty-four. She washed the glassware and kept the notebooks. She stayed twenty-five years. She did not marry. She does not take the medicine. She does not take any medicine. I once watched her sit through a migraine, which is a headache bad enough to blind you, with a wet cloth over her eyes. There was aspirin in the drawer. I recorded it as a quirk.

It began on a Wednesday in February, two years ago. We were working late on the annual filing, the long report a company must send the government each year. I will be accurate about why it began. I was not unhappy. I was not lonely. I do not get lonely. She was in the room. She had been in the room for twenty-five years. She put her hand flat on the table beside mine and left it there.
The lawyers would like me to say she started it. She put her hand on a table. I did the rest.

After that it was alternate Wednesdays, at a house I own on the coast near Pescadero. I arrived at six. She arrived at half past, in her own car. Dinner was ordered in advance from the same place. She left before seven the next morning. This happened twenty-nine times. It was in my calendar under the word “review.”
The board would like it to have been a great love, or else a weakness. The public forgives both. It was neither. It was a satisfactory use of a Wednesday.

For Helen it was something else. She cried on eleven of the twenty-nine occasions. I did not count at the time. I have counted since, for this statement. She asked questions. Did I think about her on the other Wednesdays. Had I ever been sorry about anything in my life, one thing, and would I tell her what it was. I said no to the first. To the second I said I would have to check.
The earring.

On the morning after the twenty-ninth Wednesday I drove her back from the coast house. She was not able to drive. She had her head against the window. My phone rang. It was a call I was expecting, about a factory in Ireland. I pulled onto the gravel, got out, and took it. The call went well.
When I got back in she was looking straight ahead.
She said, “Nineteen minutes.”
I said the call had been important.
She said, “I know. I timed it.”
I drove her home. She did not come again. Seven weeks later a newspaper had the calendar, the address of the house, and a photograph of the two of us at the door.
That morning I found the earring. It is gold, a plain loop. It was in the tray between the seats, where the coins go. That was five months ago. It is still there. I see it when I pay for parking.
I am told this is the detail the public wants. I am told to say it haunts me. It is an earring in a tray. I have not moved it because moving it has not come up.

To the shareholders, to the forty million, and to my wife: I have been advised to say that I am sorry. I am saying it. I understand that you are hurt. I understand it the way I understand that the share price fell. I have seen the number.
That is the statement.

The red lamp stays on. The operator does not say whether it was good. She has not spoken since she arrived. She looks at me over the top of the camera for longer than the crew ever did. Then she switches off the lamp, folds the three legs, and puts the camera in its bag. There is something else in the bag, soft and pale yellow, pushed down at the side. She zips it shut.
I thought it went well.
Somewhere in the house a phone is ringing.
from the box
NEPENTRA (nepentrine) tablets
Read all of this leaflet before you start.
Take one tablet once a week, on the same day each week. Choose a day you will remember. Most people choose the day they began.
Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. You may take it with or without food.
You do not need to feel unwell to take Nepentra. Most people who take it do not feel unwell.
Keep taking Nepentra for as long as your doctor tells you. For most people this is a long time.
Keep this leaflet. You may want to read it again.
TAKE 37
The operator hands me a glass of water and the box. I take the tablet. She takes the glass.
It is Thursday. The lamp is on.

Last Thursday I said I drove Helen back from the coast house because she was not able to drive. That was accurate. I did not say why she was not able to drive. Nobody had asked. The operator has not asked either. But the condition is that I say what I did from the beginning, and I began that morning in the middle.
Item two.
There is a song in this. I will come to it.

The twenty-ninth Wednesday began in the usual way. I arrived at six. She arrived at half past. Dinner was the usual dinner. We ate at the long table by the window. In daylight you can see the ocean from that table. It was dark.
Helen did not eat. She asked the question again. Had I checked. Was there one thing in my life I was sorry for.

I had checked. I had gone through the years in order, the way I would go through accounts. I told her the answer was no. I told her I could name the things other people would expect me to be sorry for. I offered to list them.
She said she did not need my list. She said she had kept her own for twenty-five years.

Then she told me three things. She was leaving the company. She had copies of the notebooks she kept in a farm town in the Central Valley. She was going to take them to the board, and if the board did nothing, to a newspaper.
The notebooks belong to another Thursday. For now it is enough to say that they record something the company did in that town nineteen years ago. It is true. It would cost the company a great deal.

I did not argue. She was correct on every point and she was within her rights. I said so. I believe that is what made her stand up. She took her keys and went out to her car. I went with her. I walk guests to their cars.

Her car was on the gravel beside mine. She opened the driver’s door. She did not get in. She stood in the opening with her right hand on the frame, at the top, where the door meets the roof. She said some things about my brother. They were accurate too.
My phone began to ring in my jacket.
I closed the door. Her hand was in it.

One lawyer has asked whether I knew her hand was there. He hoped I would say no. I knew where her hand was. I know where things are. I did not close the door in anger. I was not angry. She was talking and the phone was ringing, and the door was the nearest way to make one of them stop.
It is a heavy door. It broke three of the long bones in the back of her hand. I learned the number later, from the X-ray.
I opened the door. I put her in the passenger seat of my car. I fastened her seat belt, because she could not. The nearest emergency room is thirty-one minutes north. I drove at the speed limit.
The song.

She was making a noise. It was not crying. It was lower than crying and it did not stop for breath in the normal places. It was difficult to drive with. I turned on the radio. On Wednesday nights a station in San Jose plays old Persian records, and that is where the dial was. A woman was singing. It was a song my mother played in the kitchen in Shiraz [shee-RAAZ], the city in the south of Iran where I was born, on a record player with a cracked lid. I had not heard it in fifty years. I knew every word.
I sang along. I did not sing loudly. I sang the whole song, beside a woman holding her broken hand in her lap. When it ended I waited to hear what they would play next.
I do not know why I mention the song. The song is not what I did. The door is what I did.

At the hospital I told the nurse it was a car door. That was accurate. Helen said nothing. She looked at me the whole time I was speaking. They took her through. I sat in the waiting room for two hours and ten minutes and returned the call I had missed. Before I left I asked the woman at the desk whether they stamped tickets for the car park. They did.
The floor of that waiting room had been washed with something that smelled of lemons. I had not thought about that until now.

In the morning I drove her home with her hand in plaster. That is the drive I described last Thursday. Ireland, nineteen minutes, the earring. I gave it in its correct order. I only left off the front.

She never told the newspaper about the door. She gave them the calendar, the house and the photograph. She kept the door back. It is the only part I could go to prison for. I have not worked out why she kept it.
To Helen: I am sorry about your hand. I have been advised not to say that on camera, because it admits a crime. I have said it. The operator can cut it.
That is the statement.
The lamp stays on. The operator is not looking at me this time. She is looking at her own right hand, which rests on top of the camera. She turns it over once. Then she switches off the lamp.
A phone is ringing. It rings for a long time.
from the box
Before you take NEPENTRA
Tell your doctor about any other medicines you take.
Nepentra does not make you sleepy. You can drive. You can work.
You can look after children.
You will remember everything as well as you did before. Nepentra does not affect your memory.
Do not give your tablets to anyone else, even if you think they need them.
TAKE 38
The operator hands me a glass of water and the box. I take the tablet. She takes the glass. The water tastes of the glass today. I had not known that glass had a taste.
It is Thursday. The lamp is on.

Item three is older. It is nineteen years old. The board has only ever been told a false account of it, and it is larger than the first two together. Helen called it the valley. I will call it the crossing.
There is a clipboard in this one. I will come to it.
I have to begin with fog, which I did not expect to have to do.

In the Central Valley of California, in the cold months, a fog comes up off the wet ground at night. They call it tule [TOO-lee] fog, after the reeds that grow in the ditches. It is not like the fog on the coast. It does not drift. It sits on the fields as thick as wool, and a man standing at the front of his truck cannot see the back of it. It smells of wet dust and of the fertiliser they put on the cotton. I can smell it now, which is of no use to anyone.

Tres Olmos [trace OL-mose], which is Spanish for Three Elms, is a town of two thousand one hundred people in the south of that valley. It has a school, a church, a gas station, a hall where the farmers hold their meetings, and one railway line that crosses the road to the school. Nineteen years ago the crossing had a sign and no gate. A gate costs four hundred thousand dollars. The railway said the county should pay. The county said the railway should pay. They had been saying it for eleven years.

On a morning in October a school bus stopped at the sign, as the law requires. The driver opened her door to listen, as the law also requires. She heard nothing, because that fog takes sound as well as sight. She drove onto the line. The train was carrying tomatoes to a cannery.
Nine children died. The youngest was six. The oldest was eleven.

At that time the company had the medicine and did not have permission to sell it. To get permission you must run what is called a trial. You give the medicine to a few hundred people for a year, and you send the government a record of everything that happens to them. We needed a few hundred people. I will be accurate. We needed them to be people the medicine could plainly help.

My brother read about Tres Olmos in the newspaper and put the page on my desk. He did not mean what I took him to mean. He meant: look at this, how terrible. I looked at it and saw a few hundred people.

I want it understood that I believed I was doing good. I still cannot find the step where that stops being true. Those people were in the worst pain I had ever seen in one room, and I had something in a refrigerator. I drove down myself. I rented the farmers’ hall. We put in a nurse, a doctor and a coffee urn, and we called it a clinic, and it was free. Two hundred and twelve adults came in the first month. All eighteen of the parents came. One of them was a Mrs. Aguirre [ah-GEE-reh], who had lost twin boys. I had not intended to use names.
The clipboard.

Before I arrived, the parents had started a petition, which is a sheet of paper people sign to make a government do something. They wanted the gate. They needed fourteen hundred signatures to force the county to vote on it. The clipboard hung on a nail beside the till in the gas station, with a pen on a string. In the two weeks after the bus, six hundred and eleven people signed.

Here is the difficulty I had. A trial needs a quiet year. The government wants to see the same people, living the same lives, taking the same tablet every week for twelve months. Tres Olmos was not going to be quiet. Lawyers from Los Angeles were already in the motel. They wanted the parents to sue the railway, which means to take it to court for money. Reporters came every week. If the county voted on the gate there would be meetings and marches all winter. My few hundred people would scatter and the year would be wasted.
So I made the town an offer. I will say it plainly, because it is the thing I did.

The company would pay every family in the study forty thousand dollars. For the eighteen parents it would also pay for the funerals and the headstones. In return each adult signed a paper. The paper said that for the twelve months of the study they would not join a court case, would not speak to reporters, and would not take part in any public campaign. A petition is a public campaign.

I held the meeting myself, in the farmers’ hall. I was kind. I meant it. Forty thousand dollars was two years’ wages in the packing sheds. They were tired and they were poor, and I was the only person who had come to Tres Olmos with anything but questions. Every one of them signed. Mr. Aguirre signed with his left hand, because his right was holding his wife’s.
The lawyers left that week. The reporters left the week after.

Helen came down every Friday to keep the notebooks. She wrote down blood pressure, sleep and weight, because that was her job. And on her own account, because nobody had asked her to, she wrote down the number on the clipboard. I have the column by heart. Six hundred and eleven. Six hundred and forty. Six hundred and forty-four. Six hundred and forty-four. Six hundred and forty-four.
The first six hundred and forty-four was the Friday of my meeting. Nobody signed after it. That was what the paper was for.

She wrote down the vigil too. Every Friday evening the town stood at the crossing with candles. Three hundred people came the first week. By Christmas there were forty. By spring it was the priest and two grandmothers, who were over sixty-five and too old for the study. The paper did not forbid candles. I put it down to the cold.

The year was as quiet as I had paid for it to be. People went back to the fields and the packing sheds. Mrs. Aguirre was at work in the school kitchen on the eleventh day. She needed the wages. By every number the government asked for, the trial was the best anyone had seen.

In my report to the government I did not mention the forty thousand dollars or the paper. The form had no box for them. But Helen kept the notebooks, and they are in the notebooks: every payment, family by family, and a copy of the paper with every signature. Those are the notebooks she said she would take to the board.
The permission came on a Tuesday, eleven months after the bus. There was a dinner in San Francisco. My brother did not come.

On the Thursday, in the first fog of that autumn, a pickup truck drove onto the crossing at Tres Olmos without stopping at the sign. The driver was Mr. Aguirre. He was taking his daughter to school. She was seven. She was the one he had left.
People in the town said that he, of all men living, should have known to stop and look. I do not know why he did not. It was foggy and they were late for school. That is all anyone ever found out.
There was still no gate. Nobody had asked for one in eleven months. I had paid them not to.
So it was not nine. I said nine. It was nine and then two, a year apart, and I have always kept them in separate files.
I was told by telephone, at my desk. I thanked the caller. I went into the meeting I was due in.
Mrs. Aguirre was back in the school kitchen the following Monday.

Four years ago I stopped for fuel in Tres Olmos. I was driving to Los Angeles and it was on the way. The gate is there now. It was built the spring after the truck, for a reason that belongs to next Thursday. The clipboard is there too. The paper ran out eighteen years ago, and anyone in Tres Olmos has been free to sign since. It hangs on the same nail beside the till, with the pen on a new string. The top sheet has gone the colour of weak tea. Six hundred and forty-four names.
I asked the woman at the till why it was still up. She had a box by the register, the white one with the blue band. She looked at the clipboard as if I had pointed out a crack in the ceiling.
She said, “Oh, that. Nobody’s got around to taking it down.”
I paid for the fuel. I thought about signing. I am not a resident.
To the people of Tres Olmos. I find I do not have the sentence. I had one prepared. It was accurate. I will give it next week.
That is the statement.

The lamp stays on. The operator has come out from behind the camera. She has not done that before. She stands beside it with her arms at her sides and waits, as if there were more. There is not more. My left hand is moving slightly on the table. I assume the room is cold.
She switches off the lamp.
The phone rings twice and stops.
from the box
NEPENTRA and children
Nepentra is for adults.
Do not give Nepentra to anyone under eighteen. It has not been shown to work in children.
Keep the box where children cannot see it or reach it.
If a child swallows a tablet by accident, do not be alarmed. Tell your doctor.
TAKE 39
The operator hands me a glass of water and the box. I take the tablet. She takes the glass.

It is Thursday. I slept badly, which I mention only because it is new. At four this morning I was standing at the kitchen window. There is a persimmon tree in the yard that I planted the year I bought the house. A persimmon is an orange fruit the size of a fist. At this time of year the tree has dropped every leaf and kept every fruit, so that it stands in the dark hung all over with small lamps. I watched it until the light came up. I do not know what I was watching for.
The lamp is on.
Last Thursday I said I would bring the sentence for the people of Tres Olmos. It is on a card in my desk. I read it this morning. It is accurate, and I could not bring it into this room.
Item four is my brother.
There is a pair of reading glasses in this one. I will come to them. I would like to come to them slowly.

My brother was four years younger than I am. He was the other half of the company from its first day. I made the medicine and he kept the money, and he was more careful with the money than I was with the medicine. He had thick wrists and bad eyes. When his hands were wet from the sink he pushed his glasses up his nose with the back of his wrist. He did that perhaps forty times a day. I can see him doing it now. I did not ask to.

He never took the tablet, not even after the permission came. By then he and Helen were the only two in the building who did not. He said a man who makes a thing should not need it. I took that for a joke.

He wrote the cheques for Tres Olmos. There were one hundred and thirty-one families and he wrote one hundred and thirty-one cheques, forty thousand dollars each. He did not like it. He said so in the car on the way down and he said so on the way back. But he was the bookkeeper and I was his older brother, and in our family the younger brother signs what the older one puts in front of him. That was true in Shiraz and it stayed true in South San Francisco.
Then came the truck, and Mr. Aguirre, and the girl who was seven.

The week after, my brother came into my office and shut the door. He said we had to tell the government about the money and the paper. He said the gate would have been built by now if we had stayed out of that town, and a child would be at school. He was right. I have never found a way in which he was not right.

I told him what telling would cost. The permission would be taken back. The company would close. Three hundred people would lose their work. The medicine would go back into the refrigerator and nobody would ever have it. I asked him to weigh two people against millions. I thought that was a fair question. I still think it is a fair question. It is only that I can now see his face while I ask it.
He said he would tell them himself. He gave me until the end of the month.
Here is what I did.

My brother had not been sleeping. He had told me so, as a brother, late one night in my kitchen. He told me he saw the bus. He had not been in Tres Olmos that morning and he saw it anyway, every night, coming out of the fog. He told me he had started to drink so as to stop seeing it. And he told me that one night that winter he had sat in his car in his garage with the engine running, for some minutes, before he turned it off and went in to bed.
He told me those things because I was his brother.

I took them to the investors, the people whose money had built the company. I took them to a doctor the investors chose. I said that my brother was unwell, that he drank, that he had come close to harming himself, and that he could not be trusted with the company’s accounts or its name. Every word was accurate. Within the month he was removed.
And when a newspaper in Fresno at last heard about the money in Tres Olmos, I gave them the cheques. There was one signature on them. It was not mine.
So the story the public was told, the little of it that was ever told, was that a troubled bookkeeper had paid a grieving town to keep quiet, and that his older brother had found out and removed him.
His name was Siamak [see-yaa-MAK]. I had meant to get through this without it.

In March he drove to Tres Olmos. It is four hours. He stopped at the gas station first. I know because he telephoned me from there. I was in a meeting. I saw his name on the telephone and I let it ring. He left a message. It is eleven seconds long.

He says, “It’s me. I’m at the gas station. I tried to sign the thing. The girl says I’m not a resident.” Then there is some fog, if fog can be heard. Then he says, “All right,” and that is the end of it.
Then he drove to the crossing, and parked on the line, and turned off the engine.
I am going to stop for a moment. I have not needed to do that before.

The sheriff gave me his things in a clear plastic bag. A wallet. Keys. And the reading glasses, which had been in the glove box and were not even scratched. He did not need them to drive. He only needed them for numbers.

They are in the top drawer of my desk at the company. I have opened that drawer every working day for seventeen years, to take out a pen. There is a smear on the left lens, on the outside, low down. It is from the back of his wrist.
I spoke at the funeral. People said it was a fine speech. I flew back the same afternoon for a meeting at four.

The county built the gate that spring. After a third time it could do nothing else. There is a small metal plate on the post with his name on it. Across the road there is a stone with the names of the ten children and Mr. Aguirre. I am told that people driving through sometimes take my brother for the engineer who built the gate.

I still have the message. Eleven seconds. It has been moved from one telephone to the next seven times. I never asked for that. Someone in my office arranged it once and it has gone on being arranged.
To my brother.
No. I do not have that one either.
That is the statement.

The lamp stays on. The operator comes out from behind the camera and sets a second glass of water on the table by my hand. She has not done that before. She does not look at me while she does it. Her hand is not steady.
She goes back and switches off the lamp.
No phone rings. I notice that it does not.
from the box
If you want to stop taking NEPENTRA
Talk to your doctor first.
Stopping Nepentra will not harm your body.
Some people who stop find the first weeks difficult. This is expected.
Most people who stop choose to begin again within six weeks.
TAKE 40
The operator hands me a glass of water and the box. I take the tablet. I notice for the first time that she watches my throat while I swallow, the way a nurse does. She takes the glass.

It is Thursday. I did not sleep. I say that without complaint. The night was long and had a great deal in it: the persimmon tree, a dog somewhere down the canyon, the small sound the refrigerator makes when it believes nobody is listening. Towards morning the fog came over the ridge from the ocean. It poured down between the redwoods, slow and white, the way milk goes into tea, and I stood on the cold stones in my bare feet and watched it fill the yard. I am sixty-three years old. I cannot remember the last time I stood outside in bare feet.
The lamp is on.
Item five is my wife. Her name is Shirin [shee-REEN]. I will not pretend this time that I meant to keep it back.
There is a blue cup in this one. I will come to it.

This item is twenty-five years old. It belongs to the year after a certain summer. The summer is next Thursday, and I ask you to let me leave it there one week more. For today you need only this. We have a daughter. She was five. Something had happened to her the summer before, and it was my doing, and since it happened she did not sleep as other children sleep. She woke every night at the same hour, screaming, and nobody could make her believe that she was safe in her bed.

We lived then in a small rented house in the hills above the airport. The wind came up that hill every evening and worked at the eucalyptus trees until they creaked like old ships. At night the aeroplanes came in low over the bay, one behind another, with their lights on, like a string of slow beads. I used to stand at the kitchen window and count them. I have not thought of that house in twenty years, and I find I could draw you every room.

For the first weeks I was the one who sat with the child. Then, in September, I began taking the tablet, and I found that I could sleep through the screaming. So Shirin went instead. Every night she got up from our bed and went down the hall, and she sat on the floor of that room with her back against the wall until it was light. By winter she had stopped eating at the table. She ate standing at the counter, whatever the child had left. I could see the bones at the base of her throat. She had been a woman who sang while she cooked, in a low voice with a crack in it. The singing had stopped in July and I had not noticed which day.

I will be accurate about myself. I had been taking the tablet since September. So I cannot tell you that I found it hard to watch her. I found it inconvenient. That is the word that fits the man I was, and I would give a great deal this morning to be able to offer you a better one.
But I did see that she was dying of it. I could count as well as anyone. And I had a tablet in a jar that had done me a great deal of good.

I offered it to her in October. She said no. She said that hurting for the child was the one thing she still had to give her, and she would not have it taken. I thought that was foolish. I thought it was the kind of thing people say when they are too tired to think.
Here is what I did.

On the first Thursday of November I crushed one tablet under the back of a spoon and stirred it into her tea. I did it again the next Thursday. I did it for five months. Twenty-two cups. I did not ask her and I did not tell her.

The cup was blue. She had carried it from Shiraz wrapped in a headscarf, and it had been her mother’s. It was the blue of the tiles on the old mosques there, a blue with some green at the bottom of it, like deep water. It had a chip in the rim, and she always turned the chip away from her mouth.

It worked. In December she came back to our bed. In January she ate at the table. One evening in February she sang at the stove, half a song, and I stood in the hall and listened, and I thought: I have done a good thing.
In March our daughter screamed for two hours, and Shirin lay beside me with her eyes open and did not get up.
In the morning she said, “I heard her. I thought, she’ll stop.” Then she stood very still in the kitchen with the blue cup in her hand, and she looked into it.

She found the spoon that week. There was white dust in the bowl of it. She counted the tablets in my jar. She said nothing to me. For three weeks she took the tea I made her and poured it into the sink when I had left the room.

Then one night in April it came back to her. I do not know a better way to say it. I woke at three and the bed was empty, and I found her on the kitchen floor with her back against the stove and her arms around her knees. She was making a sound I had heard before only from the child.
She said, “It’s all here. The whole winter. Every night I didn’t go to her. It’s all here at once.”
I said she should come to bed.
She said, “I was alone in it. And then you took even that.”

The telephone on the wall began to ring. It was three in the morning. I stepped past my wife and answered it, because it was ringing. It was a man in Dublin who had the hour wrong. I spoke to him for some minutes about a shipment of glassware.
I remember exactly what I thought while I stood there with the receiver. I thought: she is being loud, and she will wake the child.

They left on a Saturday. Her sister drove down from Oregon. I carried the boxes out to the car. It took Shirin an hour to get our daughter into the back seat, and when she was in, Shirin got in beside her and held both her hands, and they drove away like that, the two of them in the back and nobody in the front but the sister.
The cup was on the counter, full, and the tea was cold. She had left it for me to find.

I washed it. It is in the cupboard above the kettle in this house. I have drunk my coffee from it most mornings for twenty-five years. It is a good cup. This morning I took it down and my hands would not, I could not, I put it back.
To Shirin.
It is in the room. I can tell where it is, the way you can tell where a wall is in the dark. I cannot get to it yet.
That is the statement.

The lamp stays on. The operator walks out of the room and leaves the camera running. I sit in the chair and it films me doing nothing. Down the hall I can hear the kitchen tap. It runs for a long time. When she comes back her face has been washed. She switches off the lamp.
The house is quiet. I had not known how many things in it make a noise.

If you miss a dose of NEPENTRA
Take it as soon as you remember.
If it is nearly time for your next tablet, leave out the one you missed. Do not take two.
If you have missed several doses, you may find that you do not want to take the next one.
Take it anyway.
TAKE 41
The operator hands me a glass of water and the box.

I look at the tablet in my palm for longer than I usually do. It is white and round, with a line scored across the middle. I have taken something over thirteen hundred of them. It occurs to me that I have never once tasted one. I take it. It tastes of chalk.
She takes the glass.

It is Thursday. I did not go to bed. I sat on the back step and watched the night go. In autumn there is a wind in California that comes the wrong way, out of the desert in the east, and it is warm before the sun is up. It came this morning. The hills across the canyon went from black to grey, and from grey to the colour of a lion, and the dry grass on them moved all together like the coat of something breathing. I could smell dust and sage and, very far off, smoke. It was the warmest dawn of the autumn. I knew what day it reminded me of long before I let myself say it.
The lamp is on.
Item six. There are none after it. It is the first thing, and everything I have told you on the other Thursdays stands on top of it like the floors of a building.
There is a yellow blanket in this one. I will come to it.

It was a Thursday in July, twenty-six years ago. I was thirty-seven. I was a chemist at a large company that made medicines for the heart, and I was good at it, and I was tired of making other men rich. Shirin was a nurse. On Thursdays she worked the early shift, so on Thursdays I took our daughter to the nursery, which is a school for children too small for school.

She was four. She named everything. The car was called Mister Milk, because it was white. The moon was called Mine. She sang to her shoes while she put them on, a different song for each foot, and that morning she would not wear the left one because, she said, it was in a bad mood. I carried it out to the car in my jacket pocket. I strapped her into the seat in the back. I gave her the blanket, which was yellow and had been washed so many times it was closer to the colour of butter, and she put a corner of it against her cheek and was asleep before the bottom of the hill. She always was.

I had been waiting three weeks for a telephone call. There was a man in New York with money, and he had read a paper of mine, and if he liked me I would have a company of my own. The telephone rang as I came down into the canyon. In the canyon it would not hold a call. So I did the sensible thing. I drove back up to the top of the ridge, where there was a flat place beside the road, gravel, with a wire fence and one oak tree. I parked.

I turned off the engine. I remember being careful about that. I put on the hand brake so the car could not roll. The windows were up because of the dust. I shut my door quietly, so as not to wake her.
Then I walked away along the fence towards the oak, because it was cooler there for me, and I answered the call.

I want to tell you what I could see, because I was looking at it for a long time. The whole valley was below me. The bay lay flat and silver and the salt ponds at the edge of it were red and green, like stained glass laid on the ground. The hills on the far side were the white-gold they go in July, and as the morning came on the heat lifted off them in waves, so that they seemed to be dissolving at the edges, like sugar in a glass. There was a hawk. It hung in one place over the slope for minutes at a time, not moving a feather, held up by nothing but the heat coming off the ground. I watched it while I talked. I remember thinking that I had never seen anything so sure of itself.

The call went well. The man laughed at something I said. He asked good questions and I had good answers. I walked up and down beside the fence with my free hand in my pocket, and my fingers were closed around a very small shoe, and I did not once ask myself what it was.
I was pleased. God help me. I was so pleased.
The call ran fifty-one minutes. I have the telephone record. I have had it for twenty-six years, and for twenty-six years it has been a number.
I should say that the operator is my daughter.

I do not know why I have not said it. She wrote to me in September and asked for the job, and I gave it to her. She is thirty years old. She is standing four steps from me with her hand on the camera. I have told all of it to her face. The woman, and the car door, and the town, and her uncle, and her mother on the kitchen floor. It did not seem to me to need mentioning. Five weeks ago it did not seem to me to weigh anything at all.
I will finish.

When the man in New York had said goodbye, I stood a moment longer by the oak. I was working out what I would say to Shirin. Then I walked back along the fence. The gravel was loud. The car was white in the sun and too bright to look at, and the heat coming off its roof made the air above it shake.
I saw the blanket first. It had slipped down and lay on the floor.
I am not going to tell you what her face looked like. I have the words. I have them in two languages. I find that I will not hand them to a camera.
I broke the window with a stone. The door was not locked. I have never understood why I did that.

She did not die. A man came by in a truck with water. Then there was a fire engine, and a helicopter that landed in the road, and a hospital where she lay for eleven days without opening her eyes. On the twelfth day she opened them and asked for her blanket.

The doctors said she was a miracle. They said she would be entirely herself. That was true. They did not yet know what else was true, and it is not mine to tell. She is standing here. She can tell it.
Nushin [noo-SHEEN].
I am

It appears that I am crying. I am told I did at the hospital. I do not remember what that was like, so I cannot say if this is the same.
That is not the statement. I do not have a statement.
The lamp stays on.
WHAT SHE SAID

She comes out from behind the camera. She opens the bag and takes out the soft yellow thing that has been in it since the first Thursday, and she lays it on the table between us. It is smaller than I remembered. It is the colour of butter.
Then she puts her hand into the bag again and takes out a shoe.
It is a child’s left shoe. It is red, with a strap, and the buckle is shaped like a daisy. It would fit in the palm of my hand. She sets it down beside the blanket.
“You can stop now,” she says.
It is the first thing she has said in this room. Her voice is lower than her mother’s. I have not heard it since she was nine.

“The small thing first. The tablets are chalk. Chalk and sugar. I pressed them myself in Mom’s garage, with a little machine you can buy for forty dollars. I’ve been putting them in your box since the first Thursday. You’ve taken six of mine. You haven’t had a real one in six weeks.”
I tell her that I worked that out about twenty minutes ago.
“I know. I saw your face when you tasted it.”
She sits down on the floor with her back against the wall, the way her mother used to, and pulls up her knees.

“Now I’m going to say what it does. Nobody ever has. Not you, and not the box.” She looks into the camera when she says it. “Nepentra doesn’t make you forget. You remember every single thing you ever did. It just stops them hurting. That’s the whole medicine.”
Then she looks at me.
“And you made it for me.”
I say yes.

“Tell me if I get this wrong. In most people a hurt wears off. Something terrible happens, and a year later it’s a scar, and they can touch it. The heat burned that out of me. Nothing wears off. Everything that ever happened to me is still in its first minute. I’m thirty years old and it’s ten to nine on a Thursday in July. The buckle is too hot to touch. I can hear you through the glass.”
I say she has not got it wrong.

“So you made a tablet to do for me what I can’t do for myself. Mom told me you sat with me every night for weeks, before she did. Then you went into the kitchen and made it. That’s the best thing I know about you, and I’ve kept it very carefully. You tried it on yourself first, like a good father. It worked on you. And it didn’t work on me, because there’s nothing left in me for it to work on. Forty million people, Dad. And me.”
That is the first time she has called me that since she was nine.
I ask her who told her about the others.

“Helen. She found me in the spring, after her hand. She gave me the notebooks. She told me about the door, and she said she was keeping the door back. She said if you went to prison they’d bring you your tablet every Thursday in a paper cup, and you’d do the years like a man waiting for a bus. She said prison would be wasted on you.”
She is quiet for a moment. Then she says, “Now I want to give you the part you don’t have. You’ve got the outside of that morning. The fence and the hawk. I’ve got the inside. Can I?”
I say she can.

“I woke up because it was quiet. Mister Milk had stopped. I looked out and I could see you by the tree. And I wasn’t scared, Dad. That’s the first thing I need you to know. For a long time I wasn’t scared at all. My shoe was gone, and I thought you had taken it for a walk to cheer it up. You were laughing. I thought, good, it’s working. The shoe said something funny.”
I cannot look at her, and I look at her.

“Then it got hot, and I called you, and you didn’t turn round. And I still wasn’t angry. I was four. I thought you couldn’t hear me because the shoe was talking. I decided to be patient. I remember being proud of how patient I was being. I thought you would tell Mom.”
She presses the back of her hand against her mouth and takes it away again.
“I’m still being patient. That’s what’s wrong with me. It never finished. I never got to the end of waiting for you. I’m in the middle of it right now, while I’m talking to you.”
“Nushin,” I say.

“Let me do the rest. Everybody thinks it’s only the bad things that don’t wear off. It’s everything. I was four, and I loved you the way you love somebody when you’re four. With all of it. That hasn’t worn off either. It can’t. So I can’t hate you. I’ve tried. Mom wanted me to, a little, for my own sake. I haven’t got anywhere to stand to do it from. I’m in the back seat, and I love you, and you’re not turning round. Both of those. For twenty-six years. At full size.”
She reaches up and takes the shoe off the table and holds it in both hands.

“The nurse found this in your jacket at the hospital. Mom kept it. You said you had it in your hand for fifty-one minutes. You had your fingers round it the whole time, and you never asked yourself what it was.”
“No,” I say.

“That’s what the hurt is, Dad. It’s a shoe in your pocket. It’s a small hard thing that doesn’t belong to you. Every time your hand touches it, it asks you two questions. Whose is this? Where is she? That’s all it’s for. It isn’t a punishment. It’s how you find your way back to somebody.”
She turns the shoe over. The sole is hardly worn.

“You thought you could take the hurt out of a person and leave everything else where it was. You can’t. I’d know. It’s one thing. The part of you that hurts over somebody is the same part that holds on to them. So you made a tablet that empties everybody’s pockets. And then Helen was a Wednesday to you. And Mom was a noise in the kitchen. And Uncle Siamak was a signature. And I was a house in Oregon.”
I say that it is accurate. It is the only word I have and I am ashamed of it.

So I tell her what I have believed for twenty-six years, because it is the last thing I have to put against her. I tell her that a man who keeps from doing harm only because harm hurts him afterwards is not a good man. He is a dog that has learned where the fence is. A good man would not need the pain. I tell her that I built a country full of people who do not need it, and that I thought some of them would turn out to be good anyway.
“Did they?”
I think about a clipboard on a nail.
“I don’t know,” I say. “I never looked. It didn’t weigh enough to look at.”
She nods slowly.

“Maybe it is a fence,” she says. “I don’t know what good is. I’m the wrong person to ask. I can’t do a wrong thing twice, but that isn’t goodness. That’s just me not being able to put anything down. Maybe there are people who would be kind with empty pockets. I’d like to meet one. But I watched Mom get up and go down that hall every night for a year. I asked her once what made her do it. She said, ‘I couldn’t not.’ That was all. She couldn’t not. If that’s a fence, then I think a fence is the best thing people have. I think it might be what holds the roof up.”
Neither of us says anything after that. I do not know which of us is right. I notice that I would like it to be her.
I ask her whether tonight is the punishment, then.

“No. I’m not that kind. I’d have to carry it afterwards. I’ll tell you why I came. I’ve been in that car by myself since I was four. I’m not asking you to get me out. Nobody can. I’m asking you to get in. One night. Sit in the back with me and wait for him to turn round. It has to be you. You’re the only other person who was there.”
I ask what happens after the one night.

“Nothing. I’ve got a real one in my pocket. I’ll put it on the table in the morning. You can take it and go back to being the calm man. I won’t stop you. I’ll go on being patient. I don’t get a choice about that.”
She holds out the shoe.
“Put it in your pocket.”
I take it. It weighs almost nothing. I put it in the pocket of my jacket, on the left side, where it was before. I can feel it through the cloth.
“It’ll be tonight,” she says. “The last of the real ones is leaving you. I’ll be in the chair.”
THE NIGHT
I wake on the floor of the long room and it is hot.

The grey cloth over the window is lit from behind, and it is not a cloth. It is the silver screen people put inside a car to keep the sun off the seats. The light comes through its edges white. A telephone is ringing somewhere outside. I think, I should get up and answer that, and I cannot get up, because there is a strap across my chest.
I wake.

I am standing on gravel in the dark above the ocean, and my hand is flat on the cold frame of a car door, at the top, where the door meets the roof. A man is standing beside me. He is calm. He is listening to a telephone ring in his jacket. I know what he is going to do, because I have always known where things are, and I say to him, my hand is there, you can see my hand is there. He closes the door.

It is not as I described it. I said three bones. I gave it a number. It does not have a number. It is the whole of the world arriving in one place, and under it, worse than it, is the face of a man who is waiting to see what the radio will play next.
I wake.

Fog. I am at the till of a gas station, and there is a clipboard on a nail, and the pen is swinging on its string as if someone has just let it go. Behind me in the fog there are children talking, a whole bus of them, quite close, and a woman’s voice saying sit down, sit down now, we’re nearly there. I pick up the pen. I want to sign. I want it more than I have wanted anything. The girl at the till looks at me kindly and says, you’re not a resident. From down the road my brother says, “All right.” It takes him eleven seconds. I listen to all eleven. I had only ever counted them.
I wake.

A kitchen, and aeroplanes going over like beads on a string, and somebody is on the floor with their back against the stove, making a sound. I look for her. There is nobody on the floor but me. The sound is coming out of my own mouth. It is the whole winter. It is every night somebody did not go down the hall. A telephone is ringing on the wall, and a man steps over me to answer it, and I look up as he passes and he does not look down.
I wake, and I am small.

My feet do not reach the floor. One of them has no shoe on. There is a strap over each shoulder and a buckle on my chest that is too hot to touch, and I touch it anyway, again and again, because I have seen it opened and I cannot remember how. The air is thick and tastes of plastic. The blanket has slid off my knees and I cannot reach it. I want it more than I want to breathe.
Through the glass there is a wire fence and one oak tree and a man in a white shirt.

He is walking up and down. He has one hand in his pocket. He is looking out at a valley, at a hawk, at hills that are dissolving like sugar, and he is laughing. I can hear him through the glass. I call him. I call him by the only name I have for him. He is so pleased. He does not turn round.

It is fifty-one minutes. I had the record for twenty-six years and I did not know what was on it. It is not a number. It is one minute, and then it is another minute exactly as long, and then another, and in every one of them he could turn round and he does not. I am in all of them. I do not get to skip any.

And somewhere in the middle of it, in the heat, a hand closes over mine on the buckle. It is a grown hand, a woman’s, not quite steady. She does not open the buckle. She cannot. She only keeps her hand there over mine.
She has been here the whole time. She has been here since ten to nine. She was four and then she was nine and then she was thirty, and it was always this minute, and nobody came.

It is very crowded in the car. Helen is here, holding her wrist. The ten children are here, and Mr. Aguirre, and my brother with his glasses pushed up, and Shirin with a blue cup in both hands. Everyone I ever hurt is in this car. And still it is only the two of us, a child and a child, with the windows up, waiting for a man to turn round.
I stop calling him. I hold her hand.
That is all I do, all night. It is the first thing I have done for her in twenty-one years.
THE MORNING
It is light. The cloth over the window is a cloth.

I am on the floor of the long room with my back against the wall. Every part of me aches, as if I had been carried a long way and set down badly. My daughter is asleep in the chair with her knees drawn up. I had not known that she could sleep. Her hand is hanging down over the arm of the chair, and it is six inches from mine.
I can see the persimmon tree from where I am sitting. The sun is in it. Every fruit is lit.

It is all still here. I had thought the morning might take some of it away, the way mornings do. It has not. Helen’s hand is here. The clipboard is here. The eleven seconds are here, and the blue cup, and fifty-one minutes, each one as long as it was. I know now what they weigh. I could not have told you yesterday. I can tell you to the ounce.

I understand, sitting here, that there are things I have to do. I can list them. There is a woman in a town in the valley who lost two sons, then a husband and a daughter, and who has never been told why there was no gate. There is a board. There is a government. There is a house in Oregon with a view of a river. I have never in my life felt so clearly what I ought to do. And I know why I feel it. I feel it because it hurts. I was right about that for twenty-six years. A man does the right thing because the wrong thing will not leave him alone. Being right about it does not help me at all.
On the table there is the yellow blanket.

Beside the blanket there is a glass of water and a white box with a blue band. The box is open. There is one tablet in it. It has a line scored across the middle. I do not need to taste it to know that this one is real.
She has left the camera on. The red lamp is lit.
Nushin stirs in the chair. She does not open her eyes. She says, “It’s Friday, Dad. You never took it on a Friday.”
I look at the tablet. I look at my daughter’s hand.
My own hand is in my jacket pocket. There is a small hard thing in it that does not belong to me.
The lamp is on.
THE STATEMENT

The board had asked for every Thursday’s recording, and it had all six. On the following Monday the company released a statement by its founder. It had been recorded nearly six weeks earlier. It ran four minutes.
It was Take 36.
Commentators called it measured. One called it dignified. A man on a business programme said that it was a relief, frankly, to see somebody keep his head.
By Thursday the share price had recovered the whole eleven per cent.
A teacher in Fresno got her four thousand dollars back before she was out of bed. She took her tablet with a glass of water and went to work.

GLOSSARY
Aguirre [ah-GEE-reh] — A Spanish family name.
Bina [bee-NAA] — Persian, one who sees. A family name.
Nepentra [neh-PEN-tra] — from the Greek, no grief. The medicine
Rostam makes. In the old Greek poem the Odyssey, Helen stirs a drug called nepenthes into the wine so that the men at her table can hear about their dead without weeping.
Nepentrine [neh-PEN-treen] — The chemical name printed in small letters on the box.
Nushin [noo-SHEEN] — Persian, the sweet one. A woman’s name.
Inside it is nush, the first half of nushdaru, the healing balm of the old Persian stories.

Rostam [ROS-tam] — A Persian man’s name. In the Persian Book of Kings, Rostam is the greatest of the heroes. He wounds his own child in battle without knowing who it is, and sends for the healing balm. It comes too late.
Shiraz [shee-RAAZ] — A city in the south of Iran.
Shirin [shee-REEN] — Persian, sweet. A woman’s name.
Siamak [see-yaa-MAK] — A Persian man’s name.
Tres Olmos [trace OL-mose] — Spanish, three elms. An invented farm town in the Central Valley of California.
Tule [TOO-lee] — A reed that grows in the ditches of the Central
Valley. Tule fog is the thick ground fog named for it.
